Brent Drops Below $90 as Wall Street Splits on 2027 Oil Outlook

What I Cover My focus spans the global energy landscape and the technologies reshaping it, specifically focusing on oil and gas, renewables, and tech-driven market…

Brent crude will average $80 per barrel in 2027 as geopolitics and relatively low global inventories leave much of the world vulnerable to supply disruptions, Bank of America said in a new note. Brent fell 2.9% to 89.86 dollars by 9:02 a.m. ET on Monday, and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) dropped 2.9% to 80.96 dollars.

The bank kept its 2027 Brent forecast unchanged and projected the benchmark at $70 in 2028, with WTI at $74 and $66 over the same two years. BofA named geopolitics as the main force on prices and forecast global oil demand growth of 3 million barrels per day year-on-year in both 2027 and 2028.

BofA pointed to the premium that Dated Brent, the physical North Sea benchmark, has commanded over front-month futures as "a clear indication of acute scarcity in the prompt physical market triggered by direct military attacks on energy infrastructure." Goldman Sachs says that spread has narrowed to about a $1 premium, from about $31 in early October. Goldman analysts led by Michele Della Vigna put crude freight rates in the Atlantic basin 60% to 70% below their October peak.

JPMorgan forecast lower prices, saying persistent oversupply would hold Brent in the high $70s in the first half of 2027 before easing into the high 60s in the second half and the mid-60s in 2028.

For natural gas, BofA forecast U.S. Henry Hub prices to average $3.35 per million British thermal units in 2027. It expects Dutch TTF gas to average €55 per megawatt-hour, down from about €61 in 2026.

Crude came under early pressure from an equity selloff driven by doubts over artificial intelligence. The drop followed a weekend in which Iran's Revolutionary Guards said they launched missiles and drones at U.S. military positions in Bahrain. Yemen's Houthis also claimed a direct hit on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh refinery, a claim Saudi authorities had not confirmed as of Monday morning.

President Donald Trump told Fox News that U.S. strikes could resume against Iran after the New Year if the two sides fail to reach a deal. Iran has stepped up tanker attacks in and near the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks.
